prompt: Which positioning statement is sized correctly — specific enough to be remembered, broad enough to have a real market behind it?

options.text: "I help mid-size manufacturers modernise with AI"
"I automate PO-to-invoice matching for mid-size manufacturers running NetSuite"
"I build AI tools"
"I automate PO-to-invoice matching, exclusively for the three manufacturers in Ohio I already know"

hints: Ask: could a stranger in this market read the sentence and know within two seconds if it's their problem?
Ask separately: are there enough companies in that description to build a practice on?
explanation: The NetSuite version passes both tests: a specific process (PO-to-invoice matching), a specific pain point implied by naming the ERP (NetSuite users all know this reconciliation is manual and miserable), and a market of thousands of companies. "Modernise with AI" fails the first test — nobody reading it knows what you'd actually do on Monday. "I build AI tools" fails harder. The Ohio-only version passes the specificity test and then fails the market test in the other direction — three prospects is not a pipeline, it's a client list you already have.

prompt: List two or three things you've actually built, automated, or deeply understand — real work, even unpaid or for a friend, even small. For each, write the market it belongs to and roughly how many companies fit that market (a real guess, not a shrug). Then say which one you'd lead with and why, using the two-test rule from this lesson: nameable process, real market size.
hints: If you can't name a market size even roughly, that's information — it usually means the 'market' is really just the one client you already have.
The strongest answer isn't the most technically impressive build. It's the one with the biggest addressable market behind it.
explanation: There's no single correct niche here — the exercise is the discipline of running your own experience through both filters honestly. A common failure is picking the build that felt hardest or most clever rather than the one sitting in the biggest market; cleverness doesn't get you found, a recognisable process in a real market does.

prompt: You automate delinquency-notice generation for regional credit unions. Sort each channel by how likely it is to reach a buyer who already recognises this exact pain.

categories: Reaches the industry, not the pain

items.text: A credit union operations forum thread titled 'anyone else manually formatting delinquency letters every month?'
Direct message to the ops lead after they liked a post about slow collections
A general banking-industry LinkedIn group with 90,000 members across retail banks, insurers and credit unions
items.category: Reaches the industry, not the pain

items.text: A booth at a large regional 'FinTech Innovation' conference attended mostly by vendors selling to banks
A general freelance marketplace 'AI automation' category

hints: Ask: has this person already named the exact problem, or do you have to introduce it from scratch?
A big industry group can still be the wrong room if the pain you solve is a small slice of what that group talks about.
explanation: The forum thread and the reactive DM are gold because the pain is already stated in the buyer's own words — you're not educating, you're answering. The 90,000-member banking group technically contains credit union ops people, but they're a small fraction drowned in retail banking and insurance content that has nothing to do with delinquency letters. The FinTech conference and the general marketplace reach neither the right industry consistently nor the specific pain — both are optimised for breadth, which is exactly what you don't want anymore.

prompt: True or false: because a trade-show booth reaches more exactly-right buyers per hour spent than a referral ask, it should generally be prioritised over asking existing clients for referrals.

config.statement: A trade-show booth should generally be prioritised over asking existing clients for referrals, because it reaches more of the right buyers per hour spent.
config.rubric: Accept any answer that identifies referral asks as typically higher-converting and far cheaper in real hours/dollars than a booth, while still allowing that a booth can be worth it at a later stage with a marketing budget and existing pipeline to fill.

hints: Compare actual cost: a referral ask costs minutes and no cash. A booth costs real money and a lost weekend, before any lead converts.
Compare trust at the moment of first contact: a referral arrives pre-sold on you specifically; a booth visitor is meeting you cold.
explanation: False, for a solo or early-stage practice specifically. A referral ask costs almost nothing and converts at a much higher rate because the lead arrives already trusting the referrer's judgment. A booth can absolutely be the right move later, once there's a marketing budget, a team, and a pipeline big enough that adding volume matters more than conversion rate — but reaching for it before exhausting the free, high-converting channel is a common and expensive mistake for someone just starting to find work.

prompt: A dental-practice management group posts in their Facebook community: "Does anyone else's front desk spend half of every morning just confirming tomorrow's appointments by phone? We miss so many because people don't pick up." Write the outreach message you'd send this practice owner directly, following the four-step structure from the worked example. Keep it under 90 words.
hints: Open with their own words or a close paraphrase — it's the fastest possible proof you read the actual post.
Your mechanism sentence needs one concrete number, even a modest one — 'often cuts confirmation calls by half' beats 'saves a lot of time.'
Your ask should be smaller than a call: a short video, a sample script, a one-line offer to show the flow for one day.
explanation: A strong version: opens by quoting the exact complaint ("saw your post about morning confirmation calls"), states the mechanism in one sentence (an automated SMS/voice confirmation flow that only routes to the front desk when a patient needs to actually reschedule, typically cutting call volume by half or more), offers a two-minute video or a one-day trial rather than a call, and closes with no pressure. Common weak answers open with 'I'm an AI consultant' before referencing the post at all — losing the one advantage a reactive message has over a cold one.

prompt: Put these four elements of a positioning one-pager into the order a skimming reader needs them, first to last.

items: Who this is for and the exact process (one sentence)

hints: The reader has to know it's for them before a number means anything to them.
Proof comes after the claim, to back it up — not before, when there's no claim yet to support.
explanation: Identify-the-reader has to come first, because a number or a proof point means nothing to someone who doesn't yet know if this applies to them. The before/after gives the claim shape; the proof backs the claim up; the next step is what converts attention into an actual conversation, and it has to be the smallest possible ask, per lesson three's core rule.

prompt: True or false: once you've stripped a case study of the client's name, it's automatically safe to publish, even if it includes a real screenshot of their system.

config.statement: Removing the client's name from a case study is sufficient to make it safe to publish, even alongside a real (if partially blurred) screenshot of their system.
config.rubric: Accept any answer identifying that identity can leak through means other than the name — a distinctive UI, visible partial data, industry-specific detail narrow enough to point at one company — and that recreated/synthetic artefacts are safer than real ones.

hints: Identity leaks through more than the name field — a distinctive dashboard UI, a partial number, a niche narrow enough that only one company fits it.
What's the actual risk-free alternative to a real screenshot?
explanation: False. Removing the name handles the most obvious leak, not all of them. A real screenshot can still be identifiable through its UI, visible partial data, or a niche described narrowly enough that only one company fits it ("the only regional P&C insurer using this specific claims platform," for instance). The safer move from this lesson is recreating the pattern with clearly synthetic sample data rather than editing a real artefact — it shows the identical mechanism with none of the exposure.

prompt: Match each proof source to what it actually demonstrates to a stranger evaluating you.

pairs.left: A public sandbox build against synthetic data
pairs.right: The mechanism genuinely works, checkable by clicking through it yourself

pairs.left: A teardown of a competitor's public, broken process
pairs.right: You can diagnose a real problem without needing insider access to prove it

pairs.left: A written playbook of your scoping method
pairs.right: Depth of judgment, even with zero client history to point to

pairs.left: An anonymised case study with a real metric
pairs.right: A real outcome, at the cost of specificity about who it happened for

right: That you're the cheapest option in the category
That the client was fully satisfied with every part of the engagement

hints: Each proof type trades something for something — think about what each one can and can't actually claim.
None of these four claims anything about price or overall satisfaction — notice what's missing from the list of what proof can show.
explanation: Each proof source is honest about a different, narrower claim than 'trust me, I'm good': a sandbox proves mechanism, a teardown proves diagnostic judgment without needing access, a playbook proves depth of thinking, and an anonymised case study proves a real result at the cost of identifiability. None of them claims to be the cheapest or that a client was fully satisfied — those are different claims requiring different (and riskier) kinds of evidence, like a testimonial with the client's actual consent.

prompt: On a first call, a prospective client says: "Our head of ops is really the one driving this, but final sign-off goes through our CFO, who hasn't been in any of these conversations yet." Which red flag from this lesson does this describe?

options.text: No fixed budget or success criteria
The person hiring you isn't the person who can approve scope or invoice — you'll be re-selling the work internally at every stage
A history of not paying on time
A timeline achievable only by skipping the safety-relevant stages

hints: Ask who actually holds the approval, not who's enthusiastic in the room.
This isn't about budget or timeline at all — it's about who has to be re-convinced later, by you, without being in the room now.
explanation: This is the approval-gap flag specifically: the CFO who ultimately signs off is absent from every conversation shaping the work, which means the scope agreed with the ops head can get overturned or re-litigated at invoice time by someone who never weighed in. It's not a budget problem or a payment-history problem — those are separate, equally real, flags this scenario doesn't show.

prompt: A prospective client wants a fixed two-week deadline for a project you believe genuinely needs four to do safely — including a review stage before anything touches live customer data. Write the two or three sentences you'd actually say to them, using the reframe pattern from the case study: separate what you can guarantee from what you can't, and offer to serve the real underlying need (probably urgency about something specific) a different way.
hints: What's likely driving the two-week number? Naming that out loud usually opens more room than arguing the number itself.
Could a smaller, real deliverable land in two weeks even if the full scope can't?
explanation: A strong answer names what's realistically achievable in two weeks (perhaps a scoped pilot on non-live data, or the first stage only), states plainly why the review stage before live data isn't optional, and asks what's actually driving the two-week deadline — often there's a real event behind it (a board meeting, a renewal date) that a partial, honest deliverable can serve without skipping the safety stage. A weak answer either caves to the deadline silently or argues the timeline in the abstract without addressing what the client actually needs by that date.

prompt: "I help e-commerce businesses use AI." What's wrong with this positioning statement, specifically?

options.text: It's too long
It names neither a specific process nor a market narrow enough for a reader to self-identify
E-commerce is too small a market to specialise in
It doesn't mention a specific AI model or vendor

hints: Could a reader tell within two seconds if this is their exact problem?
explanation: "E-commerce" and "use AI" are both categories, not a process — the reader has no way to know if you mean returns, ad copy, inventory forecasting, or customer support. E-commerce is a huge market, not too small; the problem is entirely specificity of process, not market size, and has nothing to do with naming a vendor.

prompt: Rewrite "I help e-commerce businesses use AI" using the process-plus-market pattern from lesson one. Invent a plausible specific process if needed.
hints: Name one process (returns, customer support triage, ad copy generation) and a market band (revenue size, platform, vertical).
explanation: A strong rewrite names a process narrow enough to be memorable and a market wide enough to matter — e.g. "I automate return-authorization triage for Shopify apparel brands doing $1-5M in revenue." There's no single right answer; the exercise is applying the pattern.

prompt: You automate expense-report coding for regional construction firms. Sort these channels.

categories: Reaches the industry, not the pain

items.text: A construction-industry accounting software (e.g. Procore-adjacent) user forum thread about manual expense coding
A large general 'Construction Industry Professionals' LinkedIn group covering safety, HR, and bidding, not accounting
items.category: Reaches the industry, not the pain

items.text: A general freelance marketplace's 'automation' category

hints: Ask whether the room is grouped by your exact pain, your general industry, or neither.
explanation: The forum thread is pre-selected — people there have already named this exact pain. The LinkedIn group reaches construction broadly but the accounting pain is a small slice of what it discusses. The general marketplace reaches neither a relevant industry consistently nor the specific pain.

prompt: True or false: a referral ask should only happen if a client explicitly offers to refer you.

config.statement: A referral ask should only happen if a client explicitly offers to refer you first.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that referral is the highest-converting channel and should be actively asked for at every project close-out, not waited for.

hints: Recall the predict-number exercise from lesson two — what share of that consultant's clients came from referral?
explanation: False. Referral was the highest-converting channel in the lesson's real example (55% of first-year clients), and it worked because it was asked for directly at every close-out, not because clients volunteered it unprompted. Waiting to be offered a referral leaves the highest-converting channel almost entirely to chance.

prompt: Which opening line follows the worked-example structure from lesson three (observed signal before mechanism)?

options.text: "I'm an AI automation consultant reaching out to see if you'd be interested in a call."
"Saw your post about manually reconciling vendor invoices every Friday — I build a tool that flags mismatches automatically."
"AI is transforming how businesses like yours operate — let's chat."
"I noticed your company exists and might benefit from AI."

hints: The correct one references something the reader actually said or did, before naming the mechanism.
explanation: Only the vendor-invoice line references an observed, specific signal before naming the mechanism — proving the sender actually looked. The others are generic enough to have been sent to anyone, which is exactly the failure mode the worked example diagnoses.

prompt: Match each proof action to whether it's safe to publish without asking the client.

pairs.left: "A regional logistics company" plus a real, specific outcome metric
pairs.right: Safe — aggregate industry description, no identifying artefact

pairs.left: The client's actual company name, used once for credibility
pairs.right: Unsafe — this is exactly what confidentiality terms exist to prevent

pairs.left: A real screenshot of their dashboard with the logo cropped out
pairs.right: Unsafe — UI and partial data can still identify them

pairs.left: A rebuilt version of the same pipeline using obviously synthetic sample data
pairs.right: Safe — same mechanism shown, nothing real exposed

right: Safe only with written client sign-off, never by default
Unsafe under any circumstances, even with permission

hints: The two distractor answers on the right don't match anything on the left — notice what's missing.
explanation: This mirrors the module's core rule: publish the pattern and the number, never the identity or the raw artefact. The two distractor options don't apply to any of the four left-hand items as stated here — sign-off could make the name option safe, but that's a different, better-documented path than 'used once for credibility.'

prompt: A prospective client says in a first call: "We're flexible on budget, we just need this done in ten days, and we'll figure out if it worked once we see it." Name which red flag(s) from lesson five apply, and what you'd say next to try to fix the situation rather than walk away immediately.
hints: "We'll figure out if it worked once we see it" is the no-fixed-endpoint flag from the diagnose-mechanism exercise.
Fixing it usually means asking a direct question that forces a fixed target, not accepting the vagueness or refusing the work outright.
explanation: This is the no-fixed-success-criteria flag (and arguably an aggressive-timeline flag alongside it). The fix, per the case-sim's lesson, is not to walk away immediately but to ask directly what a good outcome would look like in concrete terms, and propose a smaller scoped pilot with an explicit definition of done rather than proceeding on "we'll know it when we see it."

prompt: Why does an automation need a 'change-in-scope tied to data drift' clause when a one-off website build typically doesn't?

options.text: Websites never need to be updated
An automation's performance guarantee was validated against a specific snapshot of the client's data and process — if those change materially, the original guarantee no longer describes reality
It's a standard clause required by law for any software contract
It protects the client, not the contractor

hints: Think about what the original performance number (e.g. '85% confidence threshold') was actually measured against.
explanation: The performance guarantee you signed was tested against the client's data and process as they existed at handover. If the client starts selling a new product category, or changes their invoice format, the automation is now operating on inputs it was never validated against — and without this clause, you're implicitly still on the hook for the original guarantee against a business that no longer exists in the form it was tested on. This protects the contractor primarily, by making re-validation an explicit, billable trigger rather than an open-ended obligation.

prompt: Rewrite this clause to replace subjective standards with measurable ones: "The Contractor shall provide reasonable ongoing support as needed to ensure the Automation continues to perform accurately."
hints: Give 'as needed' an actual number — hours per month, or a time-boxed window.
Give 'accurately' a measurable threshold and a way it's checked (e.g. monthly sample review).
explanation: A strong rewrite specifies a bounded support commitment (e.g. "up to 4 hours per month for 90 days post-launch, covering configuration issues within the original scope") and a measurable performance definition (e.g. "flags for human review any classification below an 85% confidence score, reviewed monthly against a held-out sample; performance outside this range triggers a separate re-scoping conversation, not unlimited free support"). The key move both times is converting an open-ended promise into a bounded, checkable one.

prompt: True or false: a well-drafted liability cap will protect a consultant even if they knowingly shipped an automation without testing it, to hit a deadline.

config.statement: A liability cap protects a consultant even when they knowingly shipped an untested automation to hit a deadline.
config.rubric: Accept answers identifying that most caps carve out gross negligence or willful misconduct, and that knowingly skipping testing to hit a deadline plausibly falls into that category regardless of contract wording.

hints: Recall the carve-outs mentioned in the lesson — what typically falls outside what a cap covers?
explanation: False. Knowingly shipping untested work is the kind of decision that plausibly falls under gross negligence or willful misconduct, which most liability caps explicitly exclude — and which courts in many jurisdictions won't let a cap cover even if the contract doesn't say so explicitly. A cap protects against the ordinary, good-faith imperfection of a probabilistic system; it isn't a shield for corners you knew you were cutting.

prompt: An automation drafts customer-facing shipping-delay emails and auto-sends them with no human review. Per this lesson, what's the most practical risk mitigation — more than a bigger liability cap?

options.text: Raising the fee to cover potential damages
Adding a human-review gate before anything customer-facing goes out unreviewed
Adding more disclaimers to the email footer
Shortening the cap's coverage period

hints: What actually prevents the eleven-day pricing bug scenario from happening, rather than just capping the cost after it does?
explanation: A human-review gate prevents the damage from compounding in the first place — a bug caught on day one instead of day eleven is a much smaller problem regardless of what the contract's cap says. Raising the fee doesn't scale with realistic damages for a solo consultant, disclaimers in an email footer do essentially nothing legally or practically, and shortening a cap's coverage period doesn't address the underlying exposure at all.

prompt: Match each data-handling question to why it matters in plain terms.

pairs.left: Which third party processes the data, and where
pairs.right: The client is entitled to know a named vendor, not just 'an AI system,' is receiving their data

pairs.left: Whether the API tier trains on submitted data
pairs.right: Determines whether the client's data could resurface in another customer's model output somewhere down the line

pairs.left: What happens to the data after the engagement ends
pairs.right: Without a stated deletion timeline, data can sit indefinitely in the consultant's test environments with no defined end point

right: Determines who owns the copyright to the automation's code
Determines the consultant's hourly billing rate

hints: Each of the three real pairs maps a specific data question to a specific real-world consequence of leaving it unanswered.
explanation: Each question closes a specific, checkable gap: naming the vendor makes the exposure concrete instead of abstract, the training-data question determines whether the data could ever surface elsewhere, and a deletion timeline prevents data from lingering indefinitely with no accountability. Neither distractor relates to data handling — those are separate contract concerns (IP ownership and billing) covered elsewhere.

prompt: You prototyped a client's contract-summary tool using a free consumer AI chat interface, then plan to ship the production version on the same provider's paid API tier. Before you ship, what specifically do you need to verify, and why does the free-tier testing not answer this for you?
hints: Check the specific, current policy for the paid API tier, not the consumer product — they're often governed by different terms even from the same company.
The thing to verify is whether submitted data is used for model training, and what the deletion/retention timeline is for that specific tier.
explanation: You need to verify the API tier's current data usage and training policy directly from the vendor's documentation, specifically for that tier — many providers exclude API-tier data from training by default while their free consumer product does not, or vice versa, and policies change over time. Free-tier testing tells you the mechanism works; it tells you nothing about the data-handling terms of the different product you're about to ship on, because those are frequently governed by an entirely separate agreement.

prompt: True or false: a client who pays for an automation is entitled to own the general-purpose pipeline architecture and prompt templates the consultant reuses across all their clients, not just the client-specific configuration.

config.statement: A paying client is entitled to own the consultant's general-purpose pipeline architecture and prompt templates, not just their own specific configuration.
config.rubric: Accept answers distinguishing client-specific configuration (genuinely theirs) from the consultant's pre-existing, reusable general methodology (genuinely the consultant's, licensed for use in the deliverable), unless the contract is specifically negotiated otherwise.

hints: What did the client actually pay for — a working system for their business, or your accumulated general expertise?
The client should own everything needed to run and modify their specific system. Does that require owning your reusable underlying template too?
explanation: False by default, unless specifically negotiated. The client paid for a working system configured for their business — that's what 'ownership' should track. Your general-purpose architecture and prompt templates are pre-existing methodology you built independently and license into the deliverable; claiming otherwise (or accepting a contract that implies otherwise) means renegotiating your own expertise from zero with every new client, which is not sustainable as a business model.

prompt: You built a general-purpose 'extract line items from a messy PDF' prompt template, then configured a version of it with a specific client's field names and business rules. Under the Client Materials / Contractor IP split from this lesson, who owns what?

options.text: The client owns both the general template and the configured version
The client owns the configured version with their specific field names and rules; you retain the underlying general template, licensed to them as embedded
You own both, and the client only receives a right to use the output
Ownership is undefined unless a court decides later

hints: Recall the exact split from the lesson: 'Client Materials' versus 'Contractor IP.'
explanation: The client-specific configuration — their field names, their business rules baked in — is Client Materials, genuinely theirs. The general-purpose underlying template is Contractor IP, which you retain and license to them as embedded in the delivered system. This is the split that lets the client run and modify their system freely while you keep the ability to reuse the template's underlying structure for the next client.

prompt: A prospective client is a three-person local bakery wanting an automation for scheduling social media posts, using your already-reviewed standard template. Per this lesson, what's the right move?

options.text: Pay for a fresh lawyer review of this specific contract before signing
Use your already-reviewed template as-is — this is exactly the low-stakes, standard-terms situation it's built for
Skip a written contract entirely since the stakes are low
Have the bakery's own lawyer review it instead of yours

hints: Check this scenario against the four lines from the evidence-stack: regulated data, real financial exposure, opposing lawyer, or none of those.
explanation: None of the four lines apply here — no regulated data, low financial exposure, no opposing lawyer, and a small local relationship. This is precisely the situation a once-reviewed standard template exists for. Paying for bespoke review here misallocates a scarce resource (legal budget) away from the engagements that actually carry the risk described in the lesson; skipping a written contract entirely is a separate mistake — the fix for low stakes is a lighter contract, not no contract.

prompt: A new prospective engagement: automating patient-appointment reminder texts for a multi-location physical therapy clinic, six-figure annual contract value, and the clinic's operations director mentions their legal team will need to review anything you send. Run the four-question checklist from this lesson against this scenario and say what it tells you about how to proceed.
hints: This scenario likely trips at least two, maybe three, of the four lines from the earlier evidence-stack exercise.
Naming which specific lines it trips is more useful here than a general 'be careful' answer.
explanation: This scenario trips regulated data (patient information, plausibly covered by health-privacy regulation), real financial exposure (six-figure annual value), and an opposing lawyer (the clinic's own legal team). That's three of the four lines from the evidence-stack — a strong signal this specific engagement needs actual legal review beyond the standard reviewed template, not because the consultant's judgment is inadequate generally, but because this particular engagement crosses the thresholds where the cost of being wrong exceeds what a template can absorb.

prompt: "Contractor shall ensure the system functions properly at all times." What kind of clause is this, and why is it risky to sign?

options.text: A standard boilerplate clause with no real risk
An undefined-standard clause — 'functions properly' and 'at all times' have no measurable definition and no time boundary
A liability cap
A data processing clause

hints: Ask what would count as a violation of this clause, and who decides.
explanation: 'Functions properly at all times' is exactly the undefined-standard pattern from lesson one — no measurable threshold, no time-bounded obligation. It's not a liability cap (which bounds damages) or a data clause (which governs data handling) — it's an open-ended performance promise that needs rewriting into something measurable.

prompt: A contract has no liability cap clause at all. What's your actual exposure, in plain terms, and what's the fix?
hints: Without a cap, what bounds your liability — anything?
explanation: Without a cap, exposure is generally the client's full actual damages, uncapped — which for an automation whose output reaches money, customers, or consequential decisions could be far larger than the fee paid. The fix is adding an explicit cap, typically tied to fees paid over a defined period, with the honest understanding that most caps still won't cover gross negligence or willful misconduct.

prompt: True or false: testing an integration on a free consumer AI chat tier tells you everything you need to know about the paid API tier's data-training policy.

config.statement: Testing on a free consumer AI chat tier tells you everything you need to know about the paid API tier's data-training policy for the same provider.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that free and paid tiers are frequently governed by separate policies, and the tier actually being shipped needs to be checked directly.

hints: Recall the API-tier trap from lesson three.
explanation: False. Free and paid tiers from the same provider are frequently governed by entirely separate data-usage and training policies. Testing works the same on both — the mechanism functions identically — but that tells you nothing about the data-handling terms of the tier you actually ship on, which needs to be verified directly.

prompt: Which split correctly separates what a client owns from what a consultant retains, per this module's IP framework?

options.text: Client owns everything created during the engagement, no exceptions
Client owns their specific configuration and data integrations ('Client Materials'); consultant retains general-purpose reusable methodology ('Contractor IP'), licensed to the client as embedded
Consultant owns everything; client receives only a usage right to the final output
Ownership is always split 50/50 regardless of what was built

hints: Recall the exact two-category split from lesson four.
explanation: The Client Materials / Contractor IP split is the one from lesson four — it gives the client full ownership of everything specific to their business while letting the consultant retain and reuse their general-purpose methodology across clients, which is essential to a sustainable practice.

prompt: Sort each situation by whether it crosses a line that warrants paying for one-off legal review, per lesson five.

items.text: A six-figure, multi-year contract with a hospital system
The client's legal department sends back a redlined contract with unfamiliar terms
A $1,500 engagement automating a solo bookkeeper's client-onboarding emails
A known local nonprofit, small budget, no regulated data, standard terms

hints: Check each against the four lines: regulated data, real financial exposure, opposing lawyer, or none of those.
explanation: The hospital contract trips both regulated data and high financial exposure; the redlined contract trips the opposing-lawyer line. The bookkeeping and nonprofit engagements trip none of the four lines and are exactly what a once-reviewed standard template is for.

prompt: An automation auto-approves small refunds under $50 with no human review, and a bug causes it to run for two weeks before detection. Which clause from this module would have limited the actual dollar exposure, regardless of the bug?

options.text: The IP ownership clause
A liability cap sized appropriately to what the automation touches, or a human-review gate for unreviewed customer-facing output
The data processing clause
A payment-schedule clause

hints: This mirrors the pricing-quote scenario from lesson two directly.
explanation: This is the same shape as the nine-times-fee pricing bug from lesson two — an unreviewed, customer/money-facing automation running unchecked for an extended period. Either a properly sized liability cap or, better, a human-review gate before anything customer-facing ships unreviewed, is what actually limits or prevents this kind of exposure. IP, data processing, and payment clauses address entirely different risks.

prompt: Write one sentence for a contract's data-handling section, naming a specific (real or plausible) API vendor and tier, that would pass the vague-vendor spot-flaw test from lesson three.
hints: Name the actual vendor and tier, and state the training-data policy as a specific, checkable claim — not 'industry-standard AI tools.'
explanation: A passing sentence names a real vendor and tier and states a specific, checkable training-data policy — e.g. "Contractor will process Client data using [Vendor]'s API-tier service, which per [Vendor]'s current data usage policy excludes submitted data from model training." Anything using a vague phrase like 'industry-standard AI tools' fails, regardless of how confident it sounds.

prompt: A client's automated late-rent process files eviction paperwork strictly at the state's legal minimum notice period, with no exception path. Per this lesson, what's the actual gap worth raising with the client?

options.text: The process might be too slow compared to competitors
It's fully legal, but it removes the judgment step a human might have used to notice an unusual circumstance and pause, with no replacement for that function
The notices might contain typos
The automation should file even faster than the legal minimum

hints: Legal minimum is a floor, not a description of what's reasonable — the lesson's core distinction is about judgment, not compliance.
explanation: Legality doesn't answer the question this lesson is about. The gap is that a manual process, however imperfect, had someone who might notice an unusual circumstance (first late payment in years, a documented emergency) and pause — the fully-automated version removes that judgment step with nothing replacing it, which disproportionately affects tenants already in precarious situations.

prompt: A retail client asks you to automate customer-service email triage: auto-close any support ticket where the customer doesn't reply within 48 hours, to clear a backlog. Run the four-step map from the worked example: stated goal, who's invisible from the client's side, what judgment the manual process had, and a better-scoped version.
hints: Think about who doesn't reply within 48 hours and why — is it always because the issue resolved itself?
The better-scoped version usually keeps most of the time savings while adding a narrow human check at the specific point of highest risk.
explanation: A strong answer names the goal (clearing a support backlog), the invisible group (customers who didn't reply because they're dealing with something else — travel, hospitalization, a shared inbox — not because the issue resolved), the manual judgment (a human agent might notice a ticket about a serious issue, like a safety complaint or billing dispute, and not auto-close it regardless of reply time), and a better version (auto-close only tickets below a severity threshold, with anything flagged as a complaint, dispute, or safety issue exempted from auto-close regardless of reply silence).

prompt: Sort each monitoring request by whether it's proportionate to a specific stated need or unbounded 'capture everything' surveillance.

items.text: "We're deciding whether to hire another support agent for Q3 — show us aggregate weekly ticket volume per team, not per person"
"Track everyone's screen activity continuously, we'll figure out what to do with it later"
"We're negotiating a new client SLA — show us average response time per ticket category, aggregated"
"Give managers a live per-employee activity score so they can see who's slacking"

hints: Ask whether each request names a specific decision it would inform, or starts from 'capture everything.'
explanation: The two proportionate requests each name a specific decision (a hiring decision, an SLA negotiation) and ask for exactly the aggregate data that would inform it. The two unbounded requests either explicitly defer the purpose ('figure out what to do with it later') or aim directly at per-person judgment ('who's slacking') with no specific decision named — the shape this lesson flags as surveillance rather than scoped efficiency work.

prompt: A client asks for a dashboard showing each employee's number of Slack messages sent per day, visible to their manager, to "see who's actually engaged." Using the four questions from this lesson, write what you'd actually ask the client before agreeing to scope this.
hints: What specific decision would message-count data inform, and is message count actually a proxy for the thing they care about?
Would an aggregate, team-level version answer the same underlying question?
explanation: A strong answer asks what specific decision this would inform (and notes that message count is a poor proxy for 'engagement' — quiet, careful communicators would be penalized), whether an aggregate team-level version would serve the same purpose, and whether employees would recognise 'see who's actually engaged' as the real, disclosed purpose if asked directly. The likely conclusion, per the lesson, is that this request needs to be either dropped or substantially rescoped toward an aggregate, purpose-specific metric before any building starts.

prompt: Per this lesson, what actually determines whether a decision category is appropriate to fully automate — model accuracy, or something else?

options.text: Model accuracy alone — if it's accurate enough, full automation is appropriate
Stakes and reversibility for the person affected, and whether a protected category is disproportionately harmed — regardless of average accuracy
How expensive the human alternative is
Whether the client explicitly asked for full automation

hints: Recall the credit-denial and termination-notice examples from the evidence-stack — what made them different from spam filtering, given both can be accurate?
explanation: The evidence-stack made this explicit: spam filtering and duplicate-flagging are low-stakes and reversible, so they're fine to fully automate regardless of the exact accuracy figure. Credit denial and termination are high-stakes, hard to reverse, and disproportionately affect people already at a disadvantage — keeping a human as final decision-maker there isn't about distrust of the model's accuracy, it's about stakes and reversibility.

prompt: A client's benefits-eligibility triage model has 96% agreement with expert caseworkers and they want to remove human review for denials entirely, citing cost savings. Using the four-step structure from the worked example, write your response.
hints: Start by accepting the 96% figure as real, then ask what an average figure across all applicants hides.
Benefits eligibility likely has its own version of an explanation requirement, or at least a strong ethical case for one, even without a formal legal mandate.
explanation: A strong answer accepts the 96% figure without dispute, points out that average agreement can still hide a much higher error rate for applicants with atypical circumstances (non-standard income, disability documentation gaps, language barriers in the application), notes that benefits denials are high-stakes and often hard to reverse quickly for someone who needs the support now, and proposes keeping the model's full triage and pre-scoring speed while requiring human review specifically before any denial is finalized.

prompt: True or false: a client who already leans toward a decision before hiring you is automatically asking for cover rather than genuine advice.

config.statement: A client who already leans toward a decision before hiring you is automatically asking for cover rather than genuine advice.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that having a prior opinion is normal and healthy; the actual signal is whether disconfirming evidence would change the outcome, tested by asking directly whether a mixed or negative finding would still be useful.

hints: The lesson distinguishes 'having an opinion already' from the actual red-flag pattern — what's the real test it proposes?
explanation: False. Most engagements start with a client having some leaning — that's normal, not a red flag on its own. The actual signal from this lesson is whether disconfirming evidence would change the outcome, tested directly by asking if a mixed or negative finding would still be useful to them. A genuine advisory client says yes; only the client seeking cover hesitates or asks specifically for a positive write-up regardless of findings.

prompt: You deliver an honest analysis with real concerns about a proposed automation. The client asks you to remove the concerns section "to keep the board deck positive," while still using your name on the report. Per this lesson, what's the right response?

options.text: Remove the section — it's their document and their call how it's presented
Decline to remove genuine findings from a document carrying your name — offer to discuss how findings are framed, but not to soften or omit them
Remove the section but keep a private copy of the original for your own records
Refuse to continue the entire engagement immediately, without further conversation

hints: Recall the specific line this lesson draws: it's fine if the analysis happens to agree with the client, and separately, what's not fine once a genuine finding exists.
explanation: This is the hard line from the lesson: once a genuine finding exists, removing or softening it to make a document more convenient while your name stays attached crosses from advisory work into something else. Keeping a private copy doesn't fix the problem — the public document still misrepresents your judgment under your name. A full immediate refusal without conversation skips the chance to resolve it (the client may accept honest framing once the line is stated plainly) — the better move is holding the line on substance while staying open on presentation.

prompt: Rewrite this decline to follow the pattern from this lesson (specific concern, what would change your answer, a rescoped path if one exists): "I don't think this project is a good fit for me — it doesn't really align with my values around AI and work."
hints: What's the actual specific concern hiding behind 'doesn't align with my values'? Name the concrete thing.
Is there a version of this project you'd say yes to? If so, name it explicitly.
explanation: A strong rewrite names something concrete instead of a general values statement — e.g. "I can build the scoring model, but I'd want a human to make the final call on any denial rather than the system auto-deciding — without that, I don't think I can put my name on it. Happy to scope that version if it works for you." This states the specific issue, the specific condition that would resolve it, and a concrete path forward, rather than a vague statement the client can't act on.

prompt: Put the four parts of a clean, reusable decline message in order.

items: Name the specific concern in concrete terms
State what would change your answer, if anything would
Offer the rescoped path, if one exists
Close without a moral verdict on the client

hints: The concern has to be named before a condition can attach to it, and the path forward comes after the condition is clear.
explanation: Naming the concrete concern first gives the client something to respond to. Stating the condition next tells them exactly what would resolve it. Offering the rescoped path turns a decline into a possible next step rather than a dead end. Closing without a verdict on the client's character is what keeps the relationship intact regardless of their answer.

prompt: A client wants to auto-reject any warranty claim where the described issue doesn't keyword-match a covered-defect list, with no human review. What's the core concern, per this module?

options.text: The keyword list might be too short
It removes the human judgment step that could recognise a genuinely covered issue described in unfamiliar language, disproportionately affecting the harder-to-articulate claims
It will be too slow to implement
Warranty claims are always fraudulent so this is fine

hints: This is the same shape as the insurance claim-triage example from lesson one and lesson three.
explanation: This mirrors the insurance and benefits triage examples directly: a keyword-based auto-denial removes the human judgment step that could recognise a real, covered issue described in nonstandard language, and it does so with no reversibility for the affected customer.

prompt: True or false: a request for 'visibility into team productivity' with no specific decision named is automatically proportionate as long as the data stays internal.

config.statement: A monitoring request is proportionate as long as the collected data stays internal to the company, even without naming a specific decision it would inform.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that proportionality is about starting from a specific decision and working backward to minimum data, not about where the data is stored or who sees it.

hints: Recall the diagnose-mechanism from lesson two — what specifically made a request unbounded?
explanation: False. Staying internal doesn't address the actual test from lesson two — proportionality is about whether the request starts from a specific, named decision and works backward to minimum necessary data, not about data storage location. 'Capture everything and see what's useful' is unbounded regardless of whether the data ever leaves the company.

prompt: Which decision category, per lesson three's stakes-and-reversibility test, is most appropriate to fully automate with no human final say?

options.text: Denying a mortgage application
Flagging likely duplicate contacts in a CRM for a human to review and merge
Auto-terminating an employee based on a performance score
Auto-denying an insurance claim with no review

hints: Apply the stakes-and-reversibility test, not accuracy — which of these is low-stakes and easily reversible?
explanation: Flagging duplicates for a human to merge is low-stakes and easily reversible — an incorrect flag costs a moment of review, not a consequential outcome for a person. The other three are high-stakes, hard to reverse, and directly affect a person's finances, housing, or livelihood — all squarely in the keep-a-human-as-final-decision-maker category regardless of model accuracy.

prompt: A client's model is 88% accurate at flagging fraudulent transactions and wants to auto-freeze flagged accounts with no human review. Using the four-step structure from lesson three's worked example, write your response.
hints: Accept the accuracy figure, then name what an average figure across all account types might hide.
Account freezes are high-stakes and hard to reverse quickly for someone locked out of their own money.
explanation: A strong answer accepts the 88% figure, notes it likely hides a higher false-positive rate for certain account types (small businesses with unusual but legitimate transaction patterns, for instance), points out that a frozen account is high-stakes and hard to reverse quickly for someone who needs access to their funds, and proposes keeping the model's full flagging speed while requiring a fast human confirmation before any freeze takes effect.

prompt: A client says: "We've already told the board we're switching to full AI underwriting — we just need your report to back it up." What's the actual test to apply here?

options.text: Whether the underwriting model is technically sound
Whether a mixed or negative finding from you would still be useful to them, tested by asking directly
Whether the board has formally voted yet
Whether the fee is high enough to be worth the risk

hints: This is the cover-versus-advice pattern from lesson four.
explanation: This is the cover-versus-advice test directly: 'back it up' language after the decision is already announced is the signal, and the concrete test is asking whether a mixed or negative finding would still be useful to them. Technical soundness matters for the underlying work but doesn't address whether you're being asked for advice or cover.

prompt: Sort each client statement by whether it signals genuine advisory work or a request for cover.

items.text: "We're leaning toward this option but want to know if we're wrong before we commit"
"We just need the write-up to be positive, the decision's already made"
"If your analysis comes back mixed, that's still useful — we'd rather know now"
"We've told the board this is happening, just need your name on the recommendation"

hints: Apply the direct test from the lesson: would a mixed or negative finding still be useful to them?
explanation: The two genuine-advisory statements explicitly welcome disconfirming evidence. The two cover-seeking statements either ask directly for a predetermined positive outcome or reveal the decision is already locked in elsewhere, with your name serving as institutional backing rather than input to the decision.

prompt: Write a two-sentence decline for this situation, following the pattern from lesson five: a client wants a fully-automated layoff-selection tool with no human review of who's selected, and you're not comfortable building it without a human final decision-maker.
hints: Name the specific concern (no human review of who's selected), state the condition, and offer the rescoped version if you'd take it.
explanation: A strong answer names the specific concern (no human in the final decision), states the condition (a human must make the final call, informed by the model's input), and offers a path forward if one exists — e.g. "I can build the tool to rank and surface relevant data for a human decision-maker, but I'm not able to build a version where the system makes the final selection with no review. Happy to scope the human-in-the-loop version."

prompt: On a low-energy day, what does this module recommend as the best way to handle a needed decline?

options.text: Go silent until you have more energy, even if that takes a week
Use a short, pre-written, reusable decline structure — specific concern, condition, rescoped path — that doesn't require full energy to execute well
Write a long, thorough explanation regardless of energy cost, since the client deserves full detail
Accept the engagement as-is to avoid the conversation entirely

hints: Recall the case-sim's three options and which one actually preserved the relationship at low cost.
explanation: The case-sim showed silence damages the relationship (reads as unresponsive) and a long explanation costs more energy than it needs to for the same result. A short, structural, reusable template does the real professional work — naming the concern, the condition, and a path forward — in a form that works even on a low-capacity day.

prompt: Which stage of a typical engagement most genuinely benefits from a live, synchronous format, per this lesson?

options.text: Weekly status updates
The initial kickoff — for rapport and fast back-and-forth clarification of scope
Stage sign-off
Routine debugging sessions

hints: Which of these depends on fast, iterative back-and-forth in a way a written document genuinely can't replicate as well?
explanation: A kickoff benefits from live format because early scope misunderstandings often surface fastest through real back-and-forth conversation, and rapport genuinely helps a new relationship. Status updates, sign-off, and debugging are all things a well-structured written artefact typically handles as well or better — more precise and fully decoupled from either party's specific availability.

prompt: You currently run weekly live debugging calls for a client automation project. Redesign this into an async-native structure, using the pattern from this lesson. Be specific about the artefacts involved, not just 'we'll message instead.'
hints: Think about what a live debugging call actually accomplishes — showing the bug, explaining reproduction steps — and what artefact could do the same thing without real-time presence.
A screen recording plus written reproduction steps is the concrete example from the lesson — build your answer around a similarly specific artefact.
explanation: A strong answer replaces the live call with a specific artefact: a short screen recording showing the bug occurring, written reproduction steps, and a shared tracker entry logging the issue with its status. This preserves everything the live call actually accomplished (seeing the bug, understanding how to reproduce it) without requiring both parties to be available at the same time — and it leaves a written record neither a live call nor a vague async message would.

prompt: True or false: proposing an async-first working structure mid-engagement, right after missing a scheduled call, communicates the same thing as proposing it in the original proposal before work begins.

config.statement: Proposing an async-first structure mid-engagement, right after a missed call, communicates the same thing as proposing the identical structure in the original proposal.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that identical content lands differently depending on timing — stated up front it reads as a considered method, stated after a missed commitment it reads as a reaction or excuse.

hints: Recall the diagnose-mechanism from this lesson — what changes between the two consultants besides timing?
explanation: False. The content can be word-for-word identical, but timing changes what it signals: proposed before any commitment has been missed, it reads as a deliberate professional method with a stated benefit. Proposed right after missing a call, it reads as a reaction to a problem, however true the underlying reasoning is in both cases.

prompt: A prospective client responds to your async-first proposal language with: "We really prefer weekly calls, that's just how we work with vendors." Write your response, using the middle-position approach from this lesson.
hints: Offer a shorter, optional live touchpoint rather than either fully caving or fully refusing.
Keep the core async structure intact — the concession is in format and length, not in abandoning the resilience benefit entirely.
explanation: A strong response offers a shorter, optional check-in (e.g. 15 minutes) alongside the full async structure, rather than reverting entirely to a weekly-call default — something like: "Happy to do a short 15-minute check-in each week if that's useful alongside the written updates — I'd just note the written tracker stays the source of truth either way, so nothing depends on that call happening every single week." This meets the client's stated preference without giving up the structural resilience the async-first approach was built for.

prompt: Why does an informal mental buffer tend to get silently spent during a good week, per this lesson?

options.text: Because clients always ask for earlier delivery
Because nothing about it is visible or requires a deliberate decision to spend — it just quietly folds into an earlier promised date
Because informal buffers are always sized too small to begin with
Because consultants are generally bad at estimating

hints: Recall the predict-number statistic — roughly 2 in 10 buffers survived. What made the difference for those that did?
explanation: The core mechanism isn't sizing or estimation skill — it's visibility. An informal buffer has no separate existence from the overall estimate, so nothing stops it from being silently absorbed the moment a good week creates optimism. A visible, labeled buffer line requires a deliberate act (deleting or shrinking that line) to spend, which is exactly what makes it survive.

prompt: You're quoting a two-stage project: research and requirements gathering (honest best case: 5 days, low technical risk, client is very responsive) and build and integration (honest best case: 12 days, first time integrating with this particular client's legacy system). Apply the four-step buffer method and show your total quoted timeline.
hints: The first stage should get a smaller buffer percentage — low risk, responsive client. The second should get a larger one — high technical uncertainty with an unfamiliar system.
Show the buffer as its own separate number for each stage, not folded into the estimate.
explanation: A strong answer sizes stage one's buffer toward the lower end (roughly 25%, about 1.25 days, given low risk and a responsive client) and stage two's toward the higher end (roughly 40%, about 4.8 days, given unfamiliar legacy-system integration), presents both as explicit contingency lines rather than padded estimates, and states a rule in advance for unused buffer (e.g. it shortens the final date rather than just becoming the new informal pace). Total quoted: roughly 5 + 1.25 + 12 + 4.8 ≈ 23 days, shown with the buffer visible, not folded in.

prompt: Sort each element by whether it belongs in a required, professional incapacity message or is optional information the sender can choose to include or not.

categories: Required for the message to do its job

items.text: The revised timeline or next expected update date
items.category: Required for the message to do its job

items.text: Whether anything currently needs the client's attention
items.category: Required for the message to do its job

items.text: A specific diagnosis or symptom list
A promise that this delay won't happen again

hints: Ask which items the client structurally needs to do their own planning, versus which are extra information about you.
explanation: The client needs the timeline and whether anything requires their attention to do their own planning — those are structurally required for the message to function. A diagnosis, symptom detail, or a promise about the future are all optional: sharing them is a personal choice about the relationship, not something the message needs to be complete and professional.

prompt: Write the actual two-to-three sentence message you'd send a client this week if you woke up unable to work, following the pattern from this lesson: sent promptly and roughly rather than delayed and polished, containing the timeline, what (if anything) needs their attention, and when they'll hear next.
hints: Keep it under four sentences — the point of this exercise is proving the short version is enough, not writing a longer one.
Don't include a diagnosis or a promise about the future — those are optional and this exercise is testing the required core.
explanation: A strong answer is genuinely short — three or four sentences — states a revised timeline or next update date, names anything (or explicitly nothing) needing the client's attention right now, and gives a specific day for the next update. It should read as sendable in under two minutes, which is the actual point: the short version is sufficient, and waiting to write something longer only adds cost without adding necessary information.

prompt: True or false: quoting a fixed project fee based on the unbuffered, optimistic time estimate gives the same protection against a bad week as quoting it based on the buffered estimate from lesson three.

config.statement: A fixed fee based on the unbuffered, optimistic estimate protects a consultant from a bad week just as well as one based on the buffered estimate.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that an unbuffered fixed fee just relocates the risk from lost hourly income to unpaid overtime absorbed to hit a fixed deadline — not the same protection.

hints: If the fee is fixed but the estimate underneath it has no slack, what happens to a bad week's lost hours?
explanation: False. If the fee is fixed to an optimistic, unbuffered estimate, a bad week doesn't disappear as a cost — it turns into unpaid overtime needed to still hit the fixed deadline, which is arguably worse than hourly billing's direct pay cut, since it's invisible to the client and fully absorbed by the consultant. The protection only exists if the fee itself is sized to the buffered timeline.

prompt: A long-time hourly-billing client asks why you're proposing a fixed fee for their next project instead of continuing hourly. Write your response using the framing from this lesson — the case that doesn't require disclosing personal reasons.
hints: Frame the fixed fee's benefit to their budget specifically, not to your schedule.
The core point: with hourly, a slow week on your end becomes their bill; with a fixed fee, it doesn't.
explanation: A strong response frames the change entirely in terms of the client's benefit: a fixed fee means their total cost is known upfront and doesn't grow if a stage takes longer than expected for reasons on the consultant's side, which is a better deal for their budget than hourly billing, where a slower week becomes directly reflected in their invoice. This is true and complete without requiring any disclosure about capacity, health, or personal reasons.

prompt: Which engagement stage most genuinely benefits from being live rather than async, per this module?

options.text: Weekly progress updates
The initial kickoff, for rapport and fast scope clarification
Bug reproduction and debugging
Stage sign-off

hints: Recall lesson one's core distinction.
explanation: The kickoff genuinely benefits from live, real-time back-and-forth for rapport and catching scope misunderstandings quickly. The other three are typically better served by a well-structured written artefact.

prompt: True or false: an async-first working style should generally be introduced to a client after you've had to miss a scheduled call, so they understand why it's needed.

config.statement: An async-first structure should generally be introduced after missing a scheduled call, so the client understands the reason for it.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting the structure should be stated in the original proposal, before any commitment is missed, so it reads as a method rather than a reaction.

hints: Recall lesson two's diagnose-mechanism on timing.
explanation: False. Stated in the proposal before anything's been missed, it reads as a deliberate professional method. Introduced right after a missed call, the identical structure reads as a reaction or an excuse — timing changes the signal even when the content is the same.

prompt: A project has one stage with an honest best-case estimate of 9 days and high technical uncertainty (new API vendor, never integrated before). Apply the buffer method: pick an appropriate percentage, compute the buffer in days, and state the total quoted timeline.
hints: High technical uncertainty pushes toward the higher end of the 25-40% band.
explanation: A strong answer applies roughly 40% given the high uncertainty — about 3.6 days of buffer — for a total quoted timeline of roughly 12-13 days, shown as two separate numbers (9 days plus explicit contingency) rather than folded into a single padded estimate.

prompt: Sort each item by whether it's required in a professional incapacity message or optional information.

items.text: When the client will hear from you next
Whether anything currently needs the client's action
The specific medical cause of the delay

hints: Ask which items the client needs to plan versus which are extra personal disclosure.
explanation: The client needs to know when to expect the next update and whether anything requires their action now — those are structurally required. The specific medical cause is optional information, a personal choice separate from whether the message is professional and complete.

prompt: Why is waiting to send a 'properly composed' incapacity message until you feel better usually worse than sending a short, rough one immediately?

options.text: Because clients always assume the worst about silence
Because the client gets zero information exactly when their planning needs it most, and a 'day or two' estimate made while unwell is unreliable
Because a polished message is never actually necessary
Because clients prefer informal communication generally

hints: Recall the spot-flaw exercise from lesson four.
explanation: The real cost of waiting is the silence itself during the window the client most needs information, combined with an unreliable time estimate made under the worst conditions for estimating — not a general claim about client psychology or preference for informality.

prompt: Match each pricing structure to how directly it ties income to a specific week's hours.

pairs.right: Ties income most directly and immediately to that week's logged hours

pairs.left: Fixed fee tied to milestones, paid regardless of which week the work lands in
pairs.right: Decouples income from any specific week, as long as the (buffered) milestone timeline holds

pairs.left: Monthly retainer for availability and capped hours
pairs.right: Decouples income from any single week even more directly, across the whole month

right: Guarantees a fixed hourly rate regardless of market conditions

hints: Think about what happens to that week's or month's income if a bad week happens under each structure.
explanation: Hourly billing ties income most directly to hours logged in a specific week — a bad week is an immediate pay cut. Milestone-based fixed fees and retainers both decouple income from any single week, provided the underlying timeline (per lesson three's buffer method) actually has slack built in.

prompt: A client asks why your fixed-fee proposal costs more than what they'd expect from your hourly rate times your estimated hours. Using this module's ideas, write a response that explains the difference honestly without disclosing personal reasons.
hints: The difference is the buffer — explain what it protects for both sides, not just for you.
Connect back to lesson five's framing: budget certainty for the client, not accommodation for you.
explanation: A strong answer explains that the fixed fee includes a planned contingency for the inherent uncertainty in the type of work involved, and that in exchange the client's total cost is locked in regardless of whether a stage takes longer than expected — a benefit to their budget certainty, not just a hedge for the consultant. This mirrors the lesson's core framing: the honest business case is budget protection for the client, which happens to also protect the consultant, without needing to explain why the buffer matters personally.

prompt: Sort each kind of AI-industry news by which layer it belongs to, per this lesson's three-layer model.

categories: Capability and cost — changes at a moderate pace
Product names and marketing — changes constantly, mostly noise

items.text: Whether a high-stakes, hard-to-reverse decision should have a human as final decision-maker
A specific model's price per million tokens dropping by half
items.category: Capability and cost — changes at a moderate pace

items.text: A well-known model's context window doubling, making a previously-impossible document-length task newly feasible
items.category: Capability and cost — changes at a moderate pace

items.text: A new startup launching a rebranded wrapper around an existing API with a catchy name
items.category: Product names and marketing — changes constantly, mostly noise

hints: Ask whether each item would change how you scope an engagement, versus which specific tool implements the same underlying approach.
explanation: Whether a human should be the final decision-maker is a professional principle from earlier in this phase and barely moves regardless of model generation. Price and capability changes (cost per token, context window size) genuinely affect what's feasible and worth a periodic check. A rebranded wrapper product is mostly marketing noise around an existing capability, not a new principle or even usually a new capability.

prompt: Name one thing in your own practice (real or plausible) that belongs to each of the three layers from this lesson: a principle that wouldn't change even with a much better model, a capability/cost fact worth checking periodically, and a piece of product news you could safely ignore.
hints: The principle should be something you'd still believe even if every model tripled in capability tomorrow.
The capability/cost item should be something that, if it changed, would genuinely change a recommendation you'd make.
explanation: There's no single correct answer — the exercise is applying the three-layer distinction to your own actual practice. A common mistake is putting a capability fact in the 'principle' category (e.g. treating 'always use a human-review gate for denials' and 'this specific model is good at classification' as the same kind of fact) — they aren't, and mixing them up is exactly what leads to over-tracking the fast layer.

prompt: True or false: following a larger number of AI-focused accounts and newsletters generally makes a consultant more genuinely current than following a small, deliberately chosen set.

config.statement: Following a larger number of AI-focused sources generally makes a consultant more genuinely current than a small, deliberately chosen set.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that broad feeds are dominated by volume/hype rather than relevance, and a small set chosen specifically for relevance to one's niche filters for signal more effectively.

hints: Recall the diagnose-mechanism comparing the two consultants — what made the second one more genuinely current despite less volume?
explanation: False. A broad feed's volume is driven by what generates engagement, which correlates poorly with what's actually consequential to a specific practice. A small set of sources deliberately chosen for relevance — vendor changelogs for your actual stack, one vertical community, one accuracy-focused digest — filters for signal directly, producing better currency with less reading time.

prompt: Name your own three sources, one per category from this lesson: a vendor changelog relevant to your actual (or plausible future) practice, a vertical-specific community, and one broader industry digest. For each, say briefly why it passes the 'has it changed a recommendation recently' test.
hints: If you can't name a specific reason a source passed the test recently, that's useful information about whether it belongs in the bounded set at all.
explanation: There's no single correct set of sources — the exercise is applying the evaluation test to your own actual situation. A common weak answer names sources chosen for general interest or reputation rather than a specific, recent instance of the source changing an actual recommendation — which is exactly the distinction this lesson is trying to build.

prompt: Why does testing against one specific known past failure keep a capability test bounded to about an hour, when a broad exploration usually doesn't?

options.text: Because specific tests always run faster technically
Because a specific known failure has a built-in stopping point — either it's fixed or it isn't — while a broad exploration of new capabilities has no natural end
Because broad exploration always requires more expensive API calls
Because vendors design new capabilities to be tested quickly

hints: Ask what tells you the test is 'done' in each case.
explanation: The bound comes from having a clear, pre-defined success condition — did this specific known failure get fixed, yes or no — which a broad exploration of general capability doesn't have. Without a specific target, 'what else can this do' has no natural stopping point and tends to expand well past an hour.

prompt: Name one real or plausible past limitation from your own practice (or a hypothetical one, if you're early in your practice) that belongs on your running test-candidate list. Then write the one-sentence verdict you'd expect to write after testing a hypothetical fix against it — what would count as 'yes, this changes my recommendation' versus 'no, it doesn't'?
hints: The limitation should be specific enough that you could recognise immediately whether a new capability actually addresses it.
The verdict sentence should be checkable, not vague — 'seems better' doesn't count as a verdict.
explanation: A strong answer names a genuinely specific past limitation (not 'AI isn't good enough at X' generally) and a genuinely checkable verdict condition tied to that specific case. The exercise is testing whether the learner can apply the bounded-test discipline to their own real situation, not whether they name a particular limitation correctly — there's no single right example.

prompt: True or false: a vendor's marketing claim that a new model version fixes a known limitation is enough basis on its own to proactively contact a past client about updating their system.

config.statement: A vendor's marketing claim of improvement is sufficient basis, on its own, to proactively contact a past client about updating their system.
config.rubric: Accept answers noting that the claim needs to be personally verified via the bounded test from lesson three before being the basis for client contact.

hints: Recall the evidence-stack's distinction between a verified change and an unverified vendor claim.
explanation: False. Per the evidence-stack, an unverified vendor claim is specifically excluded from the bar for proactive contact — it needs to be verified through your own bounded test (lesson three) against the actual known limitation before it's a reliable basis for telling a client their system should change. Acting on marketing claims alone risks recommending a change that doesn't actually hold up in practice.

prompt: You recommended a client keep a manual review step for flagged transactions six months ago because the fraud-detection model's false-positive rate was too high to trust unreviewed. You've now personally verified (via the one-hour test) that a newer model version has a meaningfully lower false-positive rate on their specific transaction patterns. Write the message you'd send them, using the framing from this lesson.
hints: Name the specific original reason for the review step, state plainly that it was correct at the time, name what specifically changed (verified, not just claimed), and offer a next step.
explanation: A strong answer states the original review step was the right call given the false-positive rate at the time, names the specific verified change (a meaningfully lower false-positive rate on their actual transaction patterns, personally tested), and offers to discuss whether and how to adjust the review step — without ever implying the original advice was a mistake, since it wasn't one.

prompt: Why does this module recommend a scheduled quarterly review in addition to the reactive weekly source-check and one-hour test habits?

options.text: Because the weekly habits are unreliable and need to be double-checked
Because both reactive habits depend on an external trigger (an announcement or changelog), and an assumption nobody ever announced changing can go stale with no such trigger
Because quarterly reviews are a standard industry requirement
Because weekly habits take too much time to sustain

hints: Recall the interactive-guess from pod one — what do both earlier habits have in common that leaves a specific gap?
explanation: Both the weekly source-check and the one-hour test are reactive — they need something to trigger them (an announcement, a changelog entry). An assumption about client needs, or a default nobody has re-questioned, can go stale with no external trigger at all, which is exactly the gap a scheduled, not triggered, quarterly review is built to close.

prompt: Run the three-question quarterly review from this lesson for your own practice (real or plausible): what did a recent (or hypothetical) engagement prove wrong or incomplete, what default haven't you re-checked, and which past client conversation deserves revisiting?
hints: Keep each answer to a sentence — the review is meant to be small enough to actually complete, not a long strategic document.
explanation: There's no single correct answer — the exercise is running the actual three-question structure against your own situation. A common weak answer gives vague, unfalsifiable responses ('I should stay more current in general') rather than something specific enough to act on, which defeats the purpose of a bounded, concrete review.

prompt: Sort each announcement by which layer it belongs to, per lesson one's three-layer model.

categories: Capability and cost — changes at a moderate pace
Product names and marketing — mostly noise

items.text: A well-known API's price per token drops 30%
items.category: Capability and cost — changes at a moderate pace
